claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulation can reliably predict the size-dependent thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Molecular dynamics captures atomic diffusion and phase-transition behavior under thermal stress.
The modeled initial state consists of as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles spanning multiple sizes.
A controlled thermal ramp is applied in the molecular dynamics simulations.
The simulations use vacuum-like conditions and constant or zero external pressure.
Atomic diffusion and the evolution of phase boundaries depend on nanoparticle size.
Increasing temperature produces enhanced surface-atom mobility in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have greater surface-to-volume ratios than larger nanoparticles.
The greater surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles causes enhanced surface-atom mobility.
Enhanced surface-atom mobility causes smaller nanoparticles to undergo structural disorder or a phase transition earlier than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will reach the critical temperature for phase transition or significant disorder at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Larger modeled nanoparticles exhibit more bulk-like behavior and maintain structural stability to higher temperatures.
Oxidation and substrate effects are excluded from the proposed simulation conditions.
The simulation is expected to be accurate only in the nanoscale regime where atomistic effects dominate.
Simulation predictions can be tested against calorimetry and in-situ structural analysis by measuring transition temperatures, diffusion coefficients, and structural markers.
